set.name: Abracadabra AI glossary
set.description: Plain-English definitions of the AI, search and software terms used on abra-ca-dabra.app, each checked against primary sources.

terms.name: AI agent
terms.question: What is an AI agent?
terms.description: An AI agent is a program that uses an AI model to pick its own next step toward a goal, inside limits people set. Plain-English definition, sources and FAQs.
terms.short: An AI agent is a program that uses an AI model to choose its own next step toward a goal, such as checking a calendar or drafting a text. It works inside limits that people set.
explainer: The key word is choose. A normal program follows steps that someone wrote in advance. An agent looks at what it just found, then picks the next tool or action itself. Anthropic draws the line this way: in a workflow, the steps are set in code, and in an agent, the model directs its own process and its use of tools.

Google's glossary puts it in similar terms: software that can reason about what a person asks, then plan and carry out actions for them. In practice, the people who set it up still decide which tools it may use, what it may never send, and who can stop it.

sections.q: How is an AI agent different from a workflow?
a: A workflow repeats steps in an order you wrote down. An agent picks the order as it goes, based on what each step turns up. If you already know the steps, a workflow is often enough. Anthropic's own advice is to start with the simplest thing that works and add an agent only when the simple version falls short.

sections.q: Does an AI agent work without people?
a: It can act on its own between checkpoints, but it should not run without limits. Anthropic suggests clear stopping rules and points where the agent can pause for a person. On this site we keep a named person who can check the work and stop a send.

faqs.question: What is an AI agent in simple terms?
faqs.answer: An AI agent is a program that uses an AI model to decide its own next step toward a goal, such as looking up a booking or drafting a reply. People set the limits it works inside.

faqs.question: Is a chatbot an AI agent?
faqs.answer: Not always. A chatbot that only answers questions is not choosing actions. It becomes more like an agent when it can pick and use tools, such as a calendar or a search, to finish a task.

faqs.question: Do I need an AI agent or a workflow?
faqs.answer: If you can write the steps down in order and they rarely change, a workflow is usually enough. An agent fits work where the next step depends on what the last step found.

terms.draft: A program that looks at what it just found and then picks its own next step, such as checking a calendar or sending a text.
terms.changes: Added that an agent uses an AI model and works toward a goal inside limits people set. The draft alone would also fit a plain rule-based script.

terms.name: Generative engine optimization
terms.question: What is generative engine optimization?
terms.description: Generative engine optimization (GEO) means shaping pages so AI answer tools show and cite them. What it is, what Google says, and the research behind it.
terms.short: Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the work of shaping web pages so AI tools that write answers are more likely to show and cite them. Examples of these tools are Google's AI Overviews and Perplexity. Google says this work is still SEO.
explainer: The name comes from a research paper that called AI answer tools generative engines. These tools search the web, read a few pages, and write one answer with links to their sources. GEO asks how a page can earn a place in that answer.

Google's own guide says that, from its side, optimizing for these AI features is optimizing for search, so it is still SEO. A page must be indexed and allowed to show a snippet before Google's AI features can use it. The paper's authors tested changes such as adding sources, quotes and real numbers, and reported visibility gains of up to 40% in their test setup.

sections.q: Is GEO different from SEO?
a: Google says no, at least for Google Search. Its guide calls the AI features part of search and says the usual SEO advice still applies. Other AI tools may work in other ways, so the safe plan is one good page that serves both a list of links and a written answer.

sections.q: What does GEO work look like on a page?
a: It looks like good search work: a clear answer near the top, headings that match real questions, named sources, and facts a reader can check. Google lists files like llms.txt and splitting pages into small chunks as things you do not need for Google Search.

faqs.question: What does GEO stand for?
faqs.answer: GEO stands for generative engine optimization. It means shaping pages so AI tools that write answers are more likely to use and cite them.

faqs.question: Does Google treat GEO as separate from SEO?
faqs.answer: No. Google's guide says optimizing for its generative AI features is still SEO, and that the usual SEO best practices still apply.

faqs.question: Where did the term GEO come from?
faqs.answer: It was named in a research paper by Aggarwal and others, presented at the KDD conference. The paper measured how often a source shows up in answers written by AI search tools.

terms.changes: Kept the meaning. Replaced 'builds on SEO instead of replacing it' with what Google actually says (it is still SEO), and named example tools from the sources.

terms.name: Answer engine optimization
terms.question: What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?
terms.description: Answer engine optimization (AEO) is getting your pages used and cited in AI answers. A plain definition, how it relates to GEO, and what Google says.
terms.short: Answer engine optimization (AEO) is the work of getting your pages used and cited when an AI tool answers a question directly. Google says it is still SEO.
explainer: An answer engine replies with a written answer instead of only a list of links. AEO is the effort to be one of the sources that answer is built from, with a link back to your page.

Google's guide groups AEO with GEO. It says both terms describe work aimed at being seen in AI search, and that for Google this work is ordinary SEO. It also warns that many AEO and GEO "hacks" sold online do not match how Google Search works.

sections.q: How is AEO different from GEO?
a: In everyday use they mean almost the same thing. Google treats both as names for the same goal: being visible in AI search. We use AEO, GEO and SEO as one practice on this site.

sections.q: What helps a page get cited in an AI answer?
a: Google's advice is the same as for search: useful, original content, a clear structure, and a page Google can crawl and index with a snippet. A citation is not the same as a click, so it helps to measure both.

faqs.question: What does AEO stand for?
faqs.answer: AEO stands for answer engine optimization. It is the work of getting your pages used and cited when an AI tool writes an answer.

faqs.question: Is AEO the same as SEO?
faqs.answer: For Google Search, yes. Google says AEO and GEO are still SEO and that the usual best practices apply to its AI features.

faqs.question: Do I need a special file or markup for AEO?
faqs.answer: Not for Google. Google says you do not need new AI text files, special markup or chopped up pages to appear in its AI features.

refs.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

terms.name: Large language model
terms.question: What is a large language model (LLM)?
terms.description: A large language model (LLM) is an AI model trained on huge amounts of text that writes by predicting the next word. Plain definition, examples and limits.
terms.short: A large language model (LLM) is an AI model trained on a huge amount of text. It writes by predicting the next word, or part of a word, over and over. Google's Gemini and OpenAI's GPT models are examples.
explainer: Google's course describes an LLM as a model that predicts a token or a run of tokens, where a token can be a word, part of a word, or a single character. Strung together, those guesses become sentences and whole answers. That is why an LLM can draft a reply, sum up a page or answer a question in plain language.

Most chat tools you have heard of run on an LLM. The model does not look facts up by itself. Google's course notes that LLMs can make up wrong answers, which is why tools that cite their sources, and a person who checks the work, matter.

sections.q: How does a large language model write?
a: It predicts what comes next, one small piece at a time. Google's course calls LLMs autocomplete that can predict thousands of tokens in a row. Training on a huge amount of text teaches it which words tend to follow which.

sections.q: Can a large language model be wrong?
a: Yes. Google lists made up answers, high computing cost and bias among the known problems with LLMs. Grounding the model in real sources and having a person review the output lowers the risk.

faqs.question: What does LLM stand for?
faqs.answer: LLM stands for large language model. It is an AI model trained on a huge amount of text so it can read and write language.

faqs.question: Is ChatGPT a large language model?
faqs.answer: ChatGPT is a chat product built on OpenAI's GPT models, and those models are large language models. Google's glossary names GPT and Gemini as examples.

faqs.question: Why do large language models make mistakes?
faqs.answer: An LLM writes by predicting likely words, not by checking facts. Google's course says LLMs can hallucinate, which means their answers can contain mistakes.

refs.title: LLMs: What's a large language model?

terms.name: llms.txt
terms.question: What is llms.txt?
terms.description: llms.txt is a proposed Markdown file that gives AI tools a site summary and key links. What goes in it, where it lives, and why Google Search ignores it.
terms.short: llms.txt is a proposed file, written in Markdown, that gives AI tools a short summary of a website and links to its most useful pages. It usually sits at the site's root, at /llms.txt. Google Search says it does not use the file.
explainer: Jeremy Howard published the proposal at llmstxt.org and updated it in August 2026. The file starts with the site's name and a one line summary, then lists links with short notes. AI tools are meant to read it when they need to learn about a site, then follow only the links they need.

The newest version says the file can sit at the root or under a path, such as a docs folder, to cover just that part of the site. Google's guide says Google Search ignores llms.txt, so it neither helps nor hurts your Google rankings. Other tools may still read it.

sections.q: Does Google use llms.txt?
a: No. Google says you do not need AI text files like llms.txt to appear in Google Search or its AI features, because Google Search does not use them. It also says it is fine to keep one for other services that do.

sections.q: What goes in an llms.txt file?
a: The proposal asks for a title line, a short summary, and then lists of links, each with an optional note. An Optional section can hold links a tool may skip. This site has its own file at /llms.txt.

faqs.question: What is llms.txt used for?
faqs.answer: It gives AI tools a short, clean guide to a website: a summary plus links to the pages that matter most, so a tool can find what it needs without reading every page.

faqs.question: Does llms.txt help my Google ranking?
faqs.answer: No. Google says Google Search ignores llms.txt, so the file will neither help nor harm your visibility or rankings in Google.

faqs.question: Is llms.txt the same as robots.txt?
faqs.answer: No. robots.txt tells crawlers which pages they may visit. llms.txt is a guide that points AI tools to useful pages when they need information.

refs.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

terms.name: AI readiness
terms.question: What is AI readiness?
terms.description: AI readiness is how prepared a business is to put an AI tool to work: its data, processes, people and decisions. A plain definition and how to check it.
terms.short: AI readiness is how prepared a business is to put an AI tool to work and get value from it. It depends on the business more than the tool. That means its data, the way work gets done, its people and who makes decisions.
explainer: A business can buy a strong tool and still get little from it. AWS makes the same point in its checklist for smaller firms: readiness is not just a technology choice. It covers your information, your workflows, your people and the rules for how AI is used and checked.

On this site we score readiness in four parts: data, process, people and the decision. The goal is to find the one weak spot to fix first, before anyone pays for a tool. Our Readiness Check is one way to start. It gives you next steps for your business.

sections.q: What makes a business ready for AI?
a: The facts a job needs are in one place a system can read, the steps are written down, someone has time to check the output, and one person owns the decision. AWS's checklist names the same areas: data, workflows, people and governance.

sections.q: How do you measure AI readiness?
a: With an assessment that scores each area, so the gap is plain. AWS describes an AI readiness assessment as a structured look at data, technology, processes and people. Our Readiness Check is a different kind of tool. It gives you next steps for your business.

faqs.question: What is AI readiness in simple terms?
faqs.answer: AI readiness is how prepared a business is to use an AI tool well. It depends on its data, its processes, its people and who owns the decision, more than on the tool itself.

faqs.question: Why does AI readiness matter before buying a tool?
faqs.answer: A tool cannot fix scattered data or steps nobody wrote down. Checking readiness first shows what to fix so the tool has a real job to do.

faqs.question: How can I check my AI readiness?
faqs.answer: Use an assessment that scores data, process, people and decisions. The Abracadabra Readiness Check takes five to seven minutes. It gives you next steps for your business.

refs.title: AI readiness checklist for SMBs: A practical starting point

terms.name: Machine learning
terms.question: What is machine learning?
terms.description: Machine learning is software that learns patterns from past data and predicts on new data. A plain-English definition with Google's wording and examples.
terms.short: Machine learning is a way to build software that learns patterns from past data. It does not rely only on rules a person wrote. The trained model can then make predictions about new data, such as next month's orders.
explainer: Google's glossary defines it as a program or system that trains a model from input data, so the model can make useful predictions from new data. It works best when the new data looks like the data it learned from. If the past is a poor guide to the future, the predictions will be poor too.

Machine learning is a broad field. Large language models are one kind of machine learning model, built for text. Many business uses are smaller and plainer: a forecast of demand, a flag on a record that looks off, or an estimate with a range around it.

sections.q: How does machine learning work?
a: You give it many past examples, and training adjusts a model until its guesses match those examples well. Then you use the trained model on new cases. Testing it on data it has not seen tells you if it really learned the pattern.

sections.q: When is machine learning worth it for a business?
a: When you have enough history to learn from and a question you ask often, such as how much stock to order. If simple rules already do the job, keep the rules. We only switch to a learned model when it beats them in testing.

faqs.question: What is machine learning in simple terms?
faqs.answer: Machine learning is software that learns patterns from past data, then uses what it learned to make predictions about new data.

faqs.question: Is machine learning the same as AI?
faqs.answer: Machine learning is one part of AI. It covers systems that learn from data, including the large language models behind many chat tools.

faqs.question: How much data does machine learning need?
faqs.answer: There is no single number. It needs enough past examples that look like the cases you will predict, and you test it on data it has not seen to check it learned.

terms.draft: Software that learns patterns from past records instead of only following hand-written rules. It can then estimate something new, like a likely race time or next month's orders.
terms.changes: Added that the trained model predicts on new data like its training data (Google's definition). Dropped the race time example, which belongs to client PIRX copy.

terms.name: Gradient boosting
terms.question: What is gradient boosting?
terms.description: Gradient boosting builds one strong model from many small decision trees, each one learning from the errors left. A plain definition, sourced to Google.
terms.short: Gradient boosting is a machine learning method that builds one strong model out of many weak ones. The weak ones are usually small decision trees. Each new tree learns from the errors the model still makes. It is added in a small step to shrink them.
explainer: Google's course explains it with two kinds of model: a weak one, typically a small decision tree, and a strong one made of many weak ones added together. At each step a new weak model is trained to predict the current error, then added to the strong model to reduce it. When the weak models are decision trees, the result is called gradient boosted trees.

A setting called shrinkage scales each new tree down before it is added. Google compares it to a learning rate: smaller steps learn more slowly but help stop the model from fitting noise. Training stops at a set limit, or when results on held back data stop improving.

sections.q: Why use gradient boosting?
a: Google's course says decision forests, the family gradient boosted trees belong to, work well on table data, such as rows of past orders with a number to predict. Each new tree only has to fix what the model before it got wrong, so the model improves step by step.

sections.q: Can gradient boosting overfit?
a: Yes. Google notes that the strong model can begin to overfit, meaning it fits the training data too closely. Shrinkage and stopping when results on a separate check set get worse help prevent that.

faqs.question: What is gradient boosting in simple terms?
faqs.answer: Gradient boosting builds a model from many small decision trees, one after another. Each new tree learns from the mistakes the model still makes.

faqs.question: What are gradient boosted trees?
faqs.answer: Gradient boosted trees are gradient boosting with decision trees as the weak models. Google's course uses this name for the most common form of the method.

faqs.question: Is gradient boosting a kind of machine learning?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is a machine learning method that combines many weak models, usually small decision trees, into one stronger model.

terms.name: Schema markup and JSON-LD
terms.question: What are schema markup and JSON-LD?
terms.description: Schema markup labels what a page is about using schema.org; JSON-LD is the format Google recommends for it. Plain definitions, sources and FAQs.
terms.short: Schema markup is code added to a web page that labels what the page is about, such as an article, a product or a business. The labels come from a shared list called schema.org. JSON-LD is the format Google recommends for it. It is a block of code that machines read and visitors do not see.
explainer: Google calls this structured data: a standard way to give clear clues about a page and sort its content. Most of it uses the schema.org vocabulary, which names types like Organization, Product and FAQPage and the facts each can carry.

JSON-LD is a W3C standard for writing linked data as JSON. On a web page it sits in its own script block, apart from the text people read, which is why Google calls it the easiest format to set up and maintain. The rule that matters most: the markup must describe what is really on the page.

sections.q: Does schema markup help with AI search?
a: Google says structured data is not required for its generative AI features, and there is no special markup for them. It still recommends structured data as part of normal SEO, because it can make a page eligible for rich results.

sections.q: What is the difference between schema markup and JSON-LD?
a: Schema markup is what you say about the page, using schema.org types and properties. JSON-LD is one way to write it down. Microdata and RDFa are the other two formats Google supports.

faqs.question: What is schema markup in simple terms?
faqs.answer: Schema markup is code that tells search engines what a page is about. It might label an article, a product or a set of questions. The labels come from schema.org.

faqs.question: Why does Google recommend JSON-LD?
faqs.answer: Google says JSON-LD is the easiest format for site owners to set up and keep up at scale. It sits in its own block, so it is not mixed into the text people read.

faqs.question: Can schema markup include things not shown on the page?
faqs.answer: It should not. Google says not to add structured data about information that visitors cannot see, even if it is accurate.

terms.name: Agentic AI
terms.question: What is agentic AI?
terms.description: Agentic AI is a broad label for AI that works toward a goal with limited supervision, often through AI agents. How it differs from an AI agent.
terms.short: Agentic AI is a broad label for AI systems that can work toward a goal with limited supervision. It usually means one or more AI agents that plan steps and use tools. Sometimes several agents work together.
explainer: IBM defines agentic AI as a system that can reach a specific goal with limited supervision, made up of AI agents. In a system with many agents, each one handles part of the job and the work is coordinated. Google's glossary says agentic simply refers to the qualities agents have, such as autonomy.

The label is used loosely. Anthropic uses agentic systems to cover both fixed workflows and true agents. Vendors often use agentic AI for a large program of many agents. On this site we use the plainer phrase AI that takes actions on its own, and we ask which single job it does and who can stop it.

sections.q: What is the difference between AI agents and agentic AI?
a: An AI agent is one system that picks its own next step. Agentic AI is the wider label for AI that acts with limited supervision, which can mean one agent or many working together. Buy for the job, not the label.

sections.q: Is agentic AI the same as generative AI?
a: No. IBM explains that generative AI makes content, such as text or images, while agentic AI uses that output to reach a goal, for example by calling outside tools to finish a task.

faqs.question: What does agentic AI mean?
faqs.answer: Agentic AI means AI systems that can work toward a goal with limited supervision, usually through one or more AI agents that plan steps and use tools.

faqs.question: Is agentic AI the same as an AI agent?
faqs.answer: Not quite. An AI agent is a single system. Agentic AI is the broader label for AI that acts on its own, often built from several agents.

faqs.question: Does agentic AI need human oversight?
faqs.answer: Yes. Its ability to act on its own is the point and the risk. Clear goals, limits and a person who can review or stop the work keep it on track.

terms.name: Readiness Check
terms.question: What is the Readiness Check?
terms.description: The Readiness Check is Abracadabra's five-to-seven-minute online check for a business that wants to use AI. It gives you next steps for your business.
terms.short: The Readiness Check is Abracadabra's online check for a business that wants to put AI to work. It takes five to seven minutes. It asks about the work that slows you down, your data and workflow, where new customers come from, and how well answer engines can read your site. It gives you next steps for your business.
explainer: The check asks one question per screen. It asks about the jobs that eat your week and whether your data, your workflow, the owner and the decision can support real work. It also asks where new customers come from. Then it does a live read of your public website.
When you finish, you leave an email. It gives you next steps for your business. You can also book a thirty-minute working session if you want one.

sections.q: What does the Readiness Check ask about?
a: It asks about four areas. First is the work that slows you down and what it costs. Next is whether your data, your workflow, the owner and the decision can carry a system. Then it asks where new customers come from. Last, it reads how easily answer engines can find and quote your site.

sections.q: How is it different from an AI readiness assessment?
a: An AI readiness assessment is the general idea: a structured look at how ready a business is for AI. AWS describes one as a look at data, technology, processes and people. The Readiness Check is our own version. It also asks where new customers come from and reads your website. It gives you next steps for your business.

sections.q: Is the Readiness Check a diagnosis?
a: No. It is a working picture of the business as you describe it, plus a public read of the site. It is not medical, legal or financial advice.

faqs.question: How long does the Readiness Check take?
faqs.answer: Five to seven minutes. There is one question per screen, and you can leave and come back with the same link.

faqs.question: Do I need a website to take the Readiness Check?
faqs.answer: Near the end, the check asks for a public website so it can read it. If that read fails, you still get the rest of the report.

faqs.question: What happens after I finish the Readiness Check?
faqs.answer: You leave an email. It gives you next steps for your business. You can also book a thirty-minute working session.

terms.name: AI citation
terms.question: What is an AI citation?
terms.description: An AI citation is a link or source name an AI tool shows with its answer. What counts as one, how pages get cited, and why it is not a click.
terms.short: An AI citation is a link or source name that an AI tool shows with its answer to back up what it says. Perplexity shows numbered links, and Google's AI Overviews show links to supporting websites. Being cited is not the same as getting a click.
explainer: Answer tools such as Perplexity, ChatGPT search and Google's AI features write a reply, then point to the pages they used. Perplexity says each answer includes numbered citations that link to the original sources. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode show links to supporting websites.

For a business, a citation means an AI tool used your page as a source. But a reader may get what they need from the answer and never click. Pew found that people clicked result links less often when Google showed an AI summary. So we track citations and clicks as two different things.

sections.q: How does a page get cited by an AI tool?
a: The tool has to be able to reach and read the page. For Google, the page must be indexed and able to show with a snippet, and Google says there are no extra technical rules for AI Overviews or AI Mode. After that, a page that answers a real question in plain words gives any answer tool something worth quoting.

sections.q: Is an AI citation the same as a click?
a: No. A citation shows your page as a source. A click is when someone opens it. A person can read the answer, see your name and move on without visiting.

faqs.question: What does it mean when an AI tool cites my site?
faqs.answer: It means the tool used your page as a source for its answer and showed a link or your name next to it. It does not mean the reader opened your page.

faqs.question: Do I need special code to be cited in Google's AI features?
faqs.answer: No. Google says you do not need new machine-readable files, AI text files or special schema markup to appear in its AI features.

faqs.question: Where can I see clicks from Google's AI features?
faqs.answer: Google says clicks and impressions from AI Overviews and AI Mode are counted in the Search Console Performance report, under the Web search type.

terms.name: Business process automation (BPA)
terms.question: What is business process automation (BPA)?
terms.description: Business process automation (BPA) uses software to run the repeated steps of a business process. A plain definition, examples, and how it differs from RPA.
terms.short: Business process automation (BPA) means using software to do the repeated steps of a business job, like sending a bill to be approved. The aim is less manual work, fewer errors and the same result each time. It can run on simple rules, workflows or AI.
explainer: IBM describes a business process as a series of steps toward one goal, such as onboarding a new hire or paying a supplier. BPA hands some or all of those steps to software. It often links several systems, so data moves from one to the next without anyone typing it again.

IBM also warns that automation stalls when the steps were never written down. That is why our note on business process automation with AI starts with a written job: the steps a person already does, who checks the result, and what counts as done.

sections.q: What are examples of business process automation?
a: Sending a welcome email and setting up access for a new hire. Matching a purchase order to an invoice and sending it for approval. Routing a help desk ticket to the right person. Each one is a set of steps that runs the same way each time.

sections.q: How is BPA different from RPA and AI agents?
a: Robotic process automation (RPA) is a narrower kind of BPA. It copies what a person does in an app, like moving data from one screen to another. An AI agent picks its own next step. BPA is the wider goal of automating the process, and it can use either one, or neither.

faqs.question: What is BPA in simple terms?
faqs.answer: BPA means letting software do the repeated steps of a business job, so people spend less time copying, checking and passing work along.

faqs.question: What should a business automate first?
faqs.answer: Start with a job that repeats often, takes real time and has steps you can write down. IBM names email alerts, help desk tickets, payroll and invoicing as common starting points.

faqs.question: Does business process automation need AI?
faqs.answer: No. Many processes run on simple rules. AI helps when a step needs reading or judgment, such as sorting emails by topic, and a person should still check the output.

terms.changes: Kept the meaning. Swapped the example for IBM's invoice approval, added the goal (fewer manual steps and errors, the same way each time) and that BPA can use rules, workflows or AI. Added how it differs from RPA, per IBM.

terms.name: Custom software
terms.question: What is custom software?
terms.description: Custom software is built for one business or group of users, around how they work. How it differs from off-the-shelf software, and when to build it.
terms.short: Custom software is software built for one business or group of users, around how they already work. Off-the-shelf software is different: it is made for many buyers and sold as a ready product. Custom software makes sense when no ready product does the job well.
explainer: IBM describes custom software development as designing, building, deploying and maintaining software for a specific set of users, functions or organizations. Off-the-shelf software is built for a broad set of needs, so it can be packaged and sold to many buyers.

Neither is better by default. If a product already does the job, buying it is usually faster. Custom software earns its cost when the job is special to how your business works and the gap shows up every week. It also needs someone to look after it once it is built.

sections.q: When should a business build custom software?
a: When the job is central to how you work, no product covers it without heavy workarounds, and someone will own it after launch. If a product already covers most of the job, buy it and adjust the process a little instead.

sections.q: What does custom software look like?
a: It can be a customer app, an internal tool, a link between two systems, or an AI assistant set up for your own records. What makes it custom is who it is built for, not how big it is.

faqs.question: What is the difference between custom and off-the-shelf software?
faqs.answer: Custom software is built for one organization's needs. Off-the-shelf software is built for many buyers and sold ready to use.

faqs.question: Who looks after custom software once it is built?
faqs.answer: Someone has to. Upkeep is part of the work, so decide who will fix it, update it and pay to run it before the build starts.

terms.draft: Software built around how one business works, for a job no ready-made product covers.
terms.changes: Kept the meaning. Widened 'one business' to one business or group of users (IBM), and named the contrast with off-the-shelf software. Moved 'no ready-made product covers it' from the definition of the term to when it makes sense.

terms.name: AI visibility
terms.question: What is AI visibility?
terms.description: AI visibility is how often and how well a business shows up in answers written by AI tools. A plain definition, how to measure it, and how it relates to SEO.
terms.short: AI visibility is how often a business shows up in answers that AI tools write, and how well. It might be named, quoted or linked. There is no standard way to measure it, so each tool and report counts it in its own way.
explainer: The researchers who named generative engine optimization measured a source's visibility by how much of an AI answer drew on it and how early it showed up. Google's guide says terms like AEO and GEO describe work aimed at being visible in AI search, and that for Google this work is still SEO.

A few things shape it. AI and search crawlers must be allowed to read your pages. The pages must answer real questions in plain words. Your business details, such as your Google Business Profile, should be up to date. Our AI visibility service works on these.

sections.q: How do you measure AI visibility?
a: There is no single number. You can check how often AI tools name or link your site for the questions your buyers ask. Google says clicks and impressions from AI Overviews and AI Mode are counted in Search Console under the Web search type. Track citations and clicks apart, because they move in different ways.

sections.q: How is AI visibility different from SEO?
a: SEO is the wider work of helping search engines find, understand and show your pages. Google says the same SEO basics apply to its AI features. AI visibility is one result you watch: whether AI answers use you.

faqs.question: What is AI search visibility?
faqs.answer: It is another name for AI visibility: how much your business shows up, gets quoted or gets linked when AI tools answer questions.

faqs.question: Can I check my AI visibility?
faqs.answer: Yes, in part. Ask the AI tools your buyers use the questions they ask, and note whether you show up. Our Readiness Check also does a live read of how well answer engines can find and quote your public site.

faqs.question: Does llms.txt improve AI visibility in Google?
faqs.answer: No. Google says you do not need AI text files or special markup to appear in Google Search, including its AI features.

terms.name: Generative AI
terms.question: What is generative AI?
terms.description: Generative AI is AI that creates new text, images, audio, video or code from a request. A plain definition, examples, and how it differs from an LLM.
terms.short: Generative AI is AI that creates new content, such as text, images, audio, video or software code, in response to a request. Large language models, which write text, are the best-known kind.
explainer: IBM defines generative AI as AI that can create original content in response to a user's prompt or request. Google's machine learning glossary calls it an emerging field with no formal definition. It says most experts agree these models make content that is complex, coherent and original.

Much of the AI businesses used before was predictive: it sorted, scored or forecast things from past data. Generative AI makes something new, like a draft email or a product photo. A person should still check the output before it goes out, because it can sound sure and still be wrong.

sections.q: What are examples of generative AI?
a: Chat tools that write text, image tools that make pictures from a description, and tools that make speech, music or video. Google's glossary lists large language models and image, audio and video models as examples.

sections.q: How do businesses use generative AI?
a: For first drafts of emails, posts and reports, for summaries of long documents, and for pictures and video made from material they already have. The safe pattern is the same each time: the tool drafts, a named person checks, and only then does it go out.

faqs.question: Is generative AI the same as an LLM?
faqs.answer: No. A large language model is one kind of generative AI, the kind that writes text. Generative AI also covers models that make images, audio and video.

faqs.question: What is the difference between generative AI and an AI agent?
faqs.answer: Generative AI makes content. An AI agent uses an AI model, often a generative one, to choose and take steps toward a goal, such as checking a calendar.

faqs.question: Can generative AI make mistakes?
faqs.answer: Yes. It can write text that sounds right but is false, which Google's glossary calls a hallucination. Check facts, numbers and names before you use the output.

terms.draft: AI that makes new content, such as text, images, audio or video, from a request.
terms.changes: Draft was accurate. Added software code to the list (IBM) and named large language models as the best-known kind. The explainer adds Google's note that the field has no formal definition.

terms.name: Workflow
terms.question: What is a workflow?
terms.description: A workflow is the set of steps that takes work from start to finish in a set order. What it means in AI, and how a workflow differs from an AI agent.
terms.short: A workflow is the set of steps that takes a piece of work from start to finish, in a set order. In AI, it also means a system where an AI model and tools follow steps written in code ahead of time. That is different from an AI agent, which picks its own next step.
explainer: Merriam-Webster defines a workflow as the sequence of steps that moves a working process from beginning to end. IBM describes it as a way to manage repeated tasks that happen in a particular order, like approving an invoice.

Anthropic draws the line that matters for AI. Workflows are systems where AI models and tools run through code paths set in advance. Agents direct their own steps and tool use. Anthropic says to start with the simplest option that works, and that is often a workflow.

sections.q: What is the difference between a workflow and an AI agent?
a: In a workflow, someone wrote the order of the steps in advance, so it runs the same way each time. An AI agent decides its next step as it goes. Anthropic says workflows give predictable results for well-defined tasks, and agents fit when the job needs flexibility.

sections.q: When should a business use a workflow instead of an agent?
a: When the steps never change. If the job is the same every time, a fixed workflow is cheaper to run and easier to check. Save an agent for a job that branches in ways you cannot write down ahead of time.

faqs.question: What is an example of a workflow?
faqs.answer: An online order that sends a confirmation email, checks stock and makes a shipping label, in that order, every time.

faqs.question: What is an agentic workflow?
faqs.answer: Google's machine learning glossary uses the term for a process where an agent plans and carries out its own steps toward a goal. That is closer to an agent than to a fixed workflow.

faqs.question: Is workflow automation the same as business process automation?
faqs.answer: Workflow automation is one kind of business process automation. IBM describes it as automating a set series of tasks so each one happens in the right order.

terms.draft: A set of steps written in advance and done in the same order every time. Unlike an agent, it does not choose its own path.
terms.changes: The draft only covered the AI sense. Added the everyday meaning first (Merriam-Webster, IBM), then Anthropic's AI sense: steps written in code ahead of time. Kept the contrast with an agent.

terms.name: Answer engine
terms.question: What is an answer engine?
terms.description: An answer engine is a search tool that replies with a written answer and its sources, not only a list of links. A plain definition with examples.
terms.short: An answer engine is a search tool that replies to a question with a written answer, usually with links to its sources, instead of only a list of links. Perplexity calls itself one. Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode work in a similar way.
explainer: A classic search engine gives you a ranked list of pages to open. An answer engine reads pages for you and writes a short reply. Perplexity says it searches the web in real time, sums up what it finds and adds numbered citations that link to the original sources.

Google describes AI Overviews and AI Mode as AI-powered responses with links to supporting websites. It says the usual SEO basics apply to them. On this site we use answer engine as the plain name for this kind of tool.

sections.q: How is an answer engine different from a search engine?
a: A search engine mainly returns a list of links for you to open and compare. An answer engine writes the answer first and shows its sources beside it. Many tools now do both, so the line is blurry.

sections.q: How does a business show up in an answer engine?
a: The tool has to be able to find and read your pages, so its crawler must be allowed in. Then the page needs a clear, honest answer to a real question. For Google, the page must be indexed and able to show with a snippet.

faqs.question: Is ChatGPT an answer engine?
faqs.answer: ChatGPT search works like one. OpenAI says sites that allow its OAI-SearchBot crawler can be shown in ChatGPT search answers.

faqs.question: What is answer engine optimization?
faqs.answer: It is the work of getting your pages used and cited when an answer engine writes a reply. Google says this work is still SEO.

faqs.question: Do answer engines send visitors to my site?
faqs.answer: Some do, through the links in their answers. But an answer can name your page without the reader clicking, so count citations and clicks apart.

terms.draft: A tool that replies with a written answer instead of a list of links, such as ChatGPT search, Perplexity or Google AI Overviews.
terms.changes: Kept the meaning and added 'usually with links to its sources'. Swapped 'such as ChatGPT search' for Perplexity, which calls itself an answer engine, and said Google's AI features work in a similar way rather than claiming Google uses the term.

terms.name: Crawler
terms.question: What is a crawler?
terms.description: A crawler is a program that visits and reads web pages on its own, for a search engine or an AI company. How robots.txt and AI crawlers work.
terms.short: A crawler is a program that visits web pages on its own and reads them, usually for a search engine or an AI company. It is also called a robot or spider. Sites use a robots.txt file to tell crawlers which pages they may visit.
explainer: Google calls crawler a general term for any program that automatically finds and scans websites. Googlebot is the main one Google uses for Search. What crawlers read is how a search engine or an AI tool learns what is on your site.

AI companies run more than one crawler, and each one is a separate switch. OpenAI says OAI-SearchBot is for search, so blocking it keeps a site out of ChatGPT search answers. GPTBot collects pages that may be used to train its models. A site can allow one and block the other.

sections.q: What does robots.txt do for crawlers?
a: It is a text file at the root of a site that says which crawlers may visit which paths. The rules are a request, not a lock: the Robots Exclusion Protocol standard says crawlers are asked to follow them, and that the rules are not a form of access control. Google says its common crawlers always respect robots.txt for automatic crawls.

sections.q: Should a business block AI crawlers?
a: It depends on what you want. Blocking a search crawler can keep you out of that tool's answers. Blocking a training crawler only says your pages should not be used to train models. Decide one crawler at a time, not all at once.

faqs.question: Is a crawler the same as a bot?
faqs.answer: A crawler is one kind of bot. Google says crawlers are sometimes called robots or spiders. But not every bot is a crawler: some fill in forms or send spam.

faqs.question: What is Googlebot?
faqs.answer: Googlebot is the main crawler Google uses for Google Search. Google says it always respects robots.txt rules for automatic crawls.

faqs.question: What is the difference between OAI-SearchBot and GPTBot?
faqs.answer: OAI-SearchBot is how OpenAI finds sites for ChatGPT search. GPTBot collects pages that may be used to train OpenAI's models. Each has its own robots.txt setting.

terms.name: HQ
terms.question: What is HQ?
terms.description: HQ is Abracadabra's client workspace, where our team and digital workers do your work and nothing goes out until you approve it. How it works.
terms.short: HQ is Abracadabra's client workspace, where our team and a crew of digital workers get your work done. Each request becomes a card with a plan. Nothing reaches your folders or your social networks until it has been reviewed and you have approved it.
explainer: A request comes in by email, through the start-a-project form, or as a note on a piece in your space. A card opens on your project board with a plan for what each piece of work must make. Digital workers, which are AI agents set up for your business, build the work and file it to HQ, where it is held.

Client Services checks the work against your request, and a person on our team signs off. Then you approve each piece, ask for a change, or remove it. Finished work sits in named folders, and approved posts can be scheduled to your connected social networks.

sections.q: How does work move through HQ?
a: Request, plan, build, review, approve and deliver. Digital workers do the building, people check it, and you decide what goes out. A change request opens a new card.

sections.q: What is a digital worker in HQ?
a: It is an AI agent set up for your business with a clear role. For each card, it searches HQ's skill library for what the task needs, builds the work and files it for review. It lists the skills it used.

faqs.question: Who is HQ for?
faqs.answer: HQ is for CEOs and business owners putting AI to work across their businesses. It is the workspace where Abracadabra delivers client work.

faqs.question: Can anything be posted without my approval?
faqs.answer: No. Only finished work you have approved can be scheduled or posted. Work that is still held cannot.

faqs.question: Which social networks can HQ post to?
faqs.answer: Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, TikTok, X, YouTube, Threads, Google Business and Bluesky. You connect each account through the network's own sign-in.

faqs.question: How do I start with HQ?
faqs.answer: HQ is our client workspace, so it opens when we start work together. Begin with the Readiness Check or a project.
